newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian scientists claim wool breakthrough.
newsitem.headline: Australian scientists claim wool breakthrough.

text.p: Scientists at the University of Adelaide, South Australia, have made what they describe as a major breakthrough into unlocking the secrets of wool growth.

The Cooperative Research Centre for Premium Wool (CRC) project at the university has isolated a gene active in the wool follicle bulb which transports amino acids such as cysteine, a major constituent of wool growth, the CRC said.

If a sheep could retain higher supplies of cysteine it would produce more wool, it said. But cysteine was found in only low concentrations in the sheep's blood and in ingested food, where it was generally degraded by micro-organisisms and lost.
Scientists have been pursuing three avenues to overcome these deficiencies.
One involved genetically altering lupins to contain high levels of cysteine-rich proteins, which could be retained and not degraded.
The second involved genetically engineering sheep to contain genes from bacteria that gave sheep the capacity to produce cysteine themselves.
The third option, being utilised at the University of Adelaide, was to improve the efficiency of uptake of the cysteine which was already in the blood supply to the follicle.
The CRC wool project's research team, led by Phil Hynd, had now found the gene which could transport the cysteine from the plasma across the follicle cell membranes.
The team was now concentrating on how and why high wool producing sheep were able to extract more available cysteine from the blood supply than low wool producing animals, it said.
This could lead to the development of a simple chemical test which could distinguish the animal's potential as a wool producer, the CRC said.
An ancillary possibility could also be the development of a defleecing agent, it said.
